scope: US DOT and SITA mishandled-baggage rates, the delayed/damaged/lost split, how long delayed bags take to come back, when a delayed bag is declared lost, Montreal Convention and US domestic compensation limits, interim-expense reimbursement while a bag is delayed, and claim deadlines, for Delta, British Airways, Aer Lingus, Air Canada and Aeromexico (SLATE's markets).

statusKey.verified: read on the official/primary page itself on 2026-10-05
statusKey.secondhand: from a third-party summary (search result synthesis or guide site) because the primary page blocked the fetch (DOT/BTS pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch throughout this session) or the primary PDF could not be parsed; cross-checked against a second summary where noted

rates.scope: US marketing carriers combined, full year 2025
rates.note: DOT began reporting this metric per 100 bags enplaned (not per 1,000) starting January 2022. Figure reported as 2,431,940 mishandled of 471,047,484 enplaned.
153,022 of 40,560,183 bags mishandled; Delta ranked 10th among reporting US carriers for this period. For comparison in the same table: American 0.73, Southwest 0.32, JetBlue 0.31.

rates.scope: Global, all airlines, 2024 (SITA Baggage IT Insights 2025 edition)
rates.note: Down from 6.9 per 1,000 in 2023, despite an 8.2% rise in global air traffic.

rates.scope: Global, all airlines, 2025 (SITA Baggage IT Insights 2026 edition, published June 2026)
rates.note: A 23% year-on-year improvement from the 2024 rate; about 24 million bags mishandled worldwide in 2025 against roughly 5 billion passengers. Primary SITA page for this specific edition could not be reached directly (only secondary coverage of it was fetched).
A 26% improvement compared with 2007, per the same report family.

split.scope: Global mishandled bags by type, 2024 (SITA Baggage IT Insights 2025 edition)
split.note: 2023's damaged-or-pilfered share was 15% and delayed was 80%, per secondhand coverage; the exact split for 2025's 24 million mishandled bags was not found in any source reached in this session (see notFound).

returnTimes.unit: percent of mishandled bags (of 33.4 million) resolved and closed within 48 hours
returnTimes.note: Breakdown given on the same primary page: 25% resolved within 12 hours, 38% within 24 hours, 37% within 48 hours (bands as published; they do not sum cleanly to 66%/100%, which may reflect rounding or overlapping cumulative/discrete reporting in the source).

returnTimes.scope: Delta Air Lines checked-bag-fee refund trigger (not a return-time statistic, but Delta's own operational threshold for 'late')
returnTimes.value: 12 hours domestic; 15-30 hours international depending on flight duration
returnTimes.unit: hours after which Delta refunds the checked-bag fee if the bag was not delivered

declaredLost.note: "If your checked bag isn't found within 21 days of your arrival, it is likely lost."

Aer Lingus treats a bag as lost once delayed beyond 21 days and applies Montreal Convention liability; essential-expense reimbursements made during the 21 days are deducted from the final lost-bag settlement if the bag is never located.
Secondhand sources describe an earlier baggage-tracing form requirement (around day 3-5) but agree the bag is "automatically deemed lost" at day 21.
Secondhand only; Aeromexico's own baggage page was not reached in this session.

declaredLost.scope: Montreal Convention, general tracing norm cited across carriers
declaredLost.note: 21 days is the period consistently cited by Delta, Aer Lingus, Air Canada and Aeromexico alike as both the point a bag is deemed lost and the Article 31 written-complaint deadline for delay; British Airways' own page was not reached to confirm its specific day-count, but third-party coverage of BA describes the same 21-day Montreal norm.

limits.scope: Montreal Convention, international carriage of baggage (Article 22(2)), effective 28 December 2024
limits.note: Up from 1,288 SDR (in force since 19/28 December 2019); approximately US$2,000 or roughly EUR1,900/GBP at the time of the revision. Covers destruction, loss, damage or delay of baggage; also the ceiling for essential-expense reimbursement during a delay. Applies to UK carriers too (Montreal Convention retained in UK law post-Brexit).

limits.scope: US domestic baggage liability, 14 CFR 254.4, effective 22 January 2025
limits.note: Up from $3,800. Computed from the CPI ratio between the December 1999 base month and July 2024 (yielding $4,672.25), rounded to the nearest $100 per 14 CFR 254.6. Reviewed every two years using CPI as of July of the review year. Applies to large-aircraft domestic flight segments.

EU261 does not cover delayed, damaged or lost baggage at all; it only addresses denied boarding, cancellation and long delay to the flight itself. Baggage claims on EU carriers/EU flights are instead governed by the Montreal Convention limit above (EU Regulation 2027/97, as amended by Regulation 889/2002, applies Montreal Convention liability rules to EU carriers including on domestic routes).

limits.unit: SDR per passenger (CAA phrases it informally as "around £1,000")
limits.note: CAA's own consumer page does not name the Montreal Convention explicitly or state the SDR figure; it gives a rough sterling approximation instead. The underlying rule is the same Montreal Convention limit as above, retained in UK law.

interimExpenses.note: Reimburses reasonable out-of-pocket costs for essential clothing, toiletries and personal-care items purchased while a bag is delayed, against itemized receipts (merchant, date, items, total, payment method). No fixed daily dollar cap stated on Delta's own page.

Reimburses reasonable and necessary items bought for immediate need while away from bags (underwear/basic clothing, toiletries, essential items); secondhand sources describe a 30-day window to submit the claim with file reference, ticket/baggage receipts and original itemized receipts. BA's own page could not be reached directly in this session (not fetched successfully).

Reimburses reasonable replacement-item purchases made during a delay of up to 21 days; any such reimbursement is deducted from the final settlement if the bag is ultimately declared lost and a loss claim is paid.

interimExpenses.scope: Montreal Convention ceiling on interim/essential expenses
interimExpenses.note: Interim expense reimbursement is not a separate pot; it counts toward (and is capped by) the same Article 22(2) 1,519 SDR per-passenger limit that covers delay, loss and damage overall.

Secondhand guide sources state DOT does not permit a carrier to impose an arbitrary fixed daily dollar cap on interim-expense reimbursement for a domestic delay; DOT's own consumer page on this (airconsumer) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch and could not be read directly to confirm the exact wording.

claimDeadlines.note: Written complaint required within 7 days of receipt of checked baggage, or no action lies against the carrier (fraud excepted). Calendar days, not working days.
Written complaint required within 21 days of the baggage being placed at the passenger's disposal.

claimDeadlines.scope: Delta Air Lines, damaged bags, domestic, tickets issued after 8 October 2025
claimDeadlines.note: 6 hours of arrival (24 hours for tickets issued before that date); exceptions for mobility devices, non-apparent damage, delayed bags and unaccompanied minors.

claimDeadlines.scope: Delta Air Lines, damaged bags, international
Delta Air Lines, delayed/missing items, domestic

claimDeadlines.note: CAA phrases this as 21 days "from receiving the delayed bag," i.e. once it is finally delivered, rather than from the date it was declared lost.
